rationale: This experimental study combines a cluster-randomized coupon pricing trial across 30 villages (1,167 households) with a stated-preference discrete choice experiment and operational cost modeling for formalized pit-latrine emptying in informal settlements of Kigali, Rwanda. The primary empirical mechanism tested is pricing, fee structure (volumetric vs. flat fee), group discounts, cost recovery, and subsidy/surcharge design (fees_tariffs_subsidies), with formal private social enterprise vs. informal service delivery (regulatory_model_ownership) examined as a secondary attribute in the discrete choice experiment. Outcomes are co-equally centered on household willingness to pay and affordability relative to service delivery costs (economic_access) and actual household uptake/coverage of safe, formalized fecal sludge emptying to sustain functional on-site sanitation (effective_access), warranting a primary outcome of economic_access and 'multiple' for the multi-outcome label.
